newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: SES/ASTRA SEES CONTINUED SATELLITE SALES GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: SES/ASTRA SEES CONTINUED SATELLITE SALES GROWTH.

text.p: The satellite operating industry is becoming increasingly competitive, but Luxembourg's Societe Europeenne des Satellites (SES) is confident revenue growth will continue.
"If the next satellite launches are a success there is no reason why turnover should not continue to grow at the same rate," Yves Feltes, SES spokesman, told Reuters on Thursday.
Sales rose by 37 percent in 1996 to 14.1 billion Luxembourg francs ($370.1 million) while net profit jumped by 67 percent to 4.8 billion.
Feltes gave no profit forecast for 1997.
SES invested 13.3 billion francs in new craft and ground operations for its Astra network last year.
"In the future there is a need for investment in replacement spacecraft and we are also investigating additional ways to develop the Astra system," Feltes said.
The first Astra 1A satellite has been in orbit since 1988 and is expected to last 12.5 years. For subsequent craft the lifespan increases to 14 or 15 years.
The lifespan is dictated by the amount of fuel on board the satellite, which is used up gradually as technicians on the ground fire its boosters to keep it in the right position.
SES is unique in having its six satellites positioned in adjacent frequencies at one site, 19.2 degrees east, which means customers need just one dish to receive their transmissions.
This so-called co-positioning concept is being copied, Feltes said, increasing competitive pressure on SES.

With no more Ku-band frequency left at 19.2 degrees east, SES is opening a second position at 28.2 degrees east where it is sending Astra 2A in December and Astra 2B late 1998. By the end of 1998 Astra will have 10 space craft.

Feltes said the company would develop orbit positions aimed at specific linguistic markets. The second position will target Britain and Ireland. BSkyB is taking 14 transponders on Astra 2A for their digital package next year.
SES embarked on digital transmission last year, introducing it in France, Germany, Scandinavia, and Benelux.
The digital signals are less prone to interference than analogue ones. On average eight digital channels fit into one transponder, compared to just one analogue channel.
Deutsche Bank Luxembourg, which helped found SES and is a subsidiary of Germany's Deutsche Bank AG, has 4.24 percent in SES. Two Luxembourg state banks hold 20 percent.
